item.title: Evaluating ice shelf basal melt rates in the Southern Ocean high-resolution model against satellite remote sensing
item.dc:creator: Andy Dinh, Eric J. Rignot, Matthew R. Mazloff, Ian G. Fenty
item.description:
Frontiers in Marine Science — matched: ice sheet, ice shelf, grounding line, Antarctica, basal melt, Southern Ocean, sea level, sea-level rise, remote sensing
Ice shelf melt rates by a warm ocean have a critical impact on ice sheet mass balance in Antarctica and in turn on the rates of sea level rise. Validating and tuning modeled ice shelf melt rates is a challenge. Here we discuss the issues by presenting validation of melt rates calculated from the Southern Ocean high-resolution model (SOhi) over the year 2007. SOhi includes full physics, tides, and an updated bathymetric compilation. We compare the model results to two satellite-derived estimates. Overall, we find that the model overestimates ice shelf melt, which we attribute to the ocean model initial (warm) conditions in some areas, bathymetric uncertainties in others, simplified physics on some ice shelves, and also to the inherent limitations of the satellite-derived estimates. The SOhi model nevertheless provides a comprehensive, detailed mapping of ice shelf melt rates around Antarctica; it captures higher melt near grounding lines and ice fronts, areas of freezing versus areas of high melt water production. The identified discrepancies between model and satellite-estimates provide guidelines for model improvements, requirements for additional observations of ice shelf cavities, and assembling of calibration/validation datasets to constrain the models.

item.title: SURFACE OCEANOGRAPHIC VARIABILITY DURING THE LAST GLACIAL MAXIMUM AND LATE HOLOCENE IN THE INDONESIAN MARITIME CONTINENT
item.dc:creator: Daffa Mazdhania, Sandy Herho, Iwan P. Anwar, Marfasran Hendrizan, Siti Kaban, Faruq Khadami, … (+2)
item.description:
BULLETIN OF THE MARINE GEOLOGY — matched: sea surface temperature, paleoclimate, last glacial maximum, LGM, interglacial, Holocene, data assimilation
This study provides a statistical characterization of surface oceanography in the Indonesian Maritime Continent (IMC) during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM; 23–19 ka) and Late Holocene (LH; 4–0 ka). Using the lgmDA v2.1 paleoclimate data assimilation product, we analyze sea surface temperature (SST), sea surface salinity (SSS), and seawater $\delta^{18}$O. Results indicate the LGM was significantly cooler, saltier, and isotopically enriched, with reduced spatial heterogeneity compared to the LH. Comprehensive nonparametric testing confirms these differences reflect fundamental changes in distributional properties, not merely mean-state shifts. The findings suggest a major oceanographic regime shift, likely driven by lower sea levels, a weakened ITF, enhanced stratification, and a drier regional climate during the LGM. This work offers a statistical framework for understanding IMC sensitivity to glacial-interglacial forcing.

item.title: Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition and their implications on the carbon cycle
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zammit, Caroline H. Lear, Lucas Joost Lourens, Paul Nicholas Pearson, Amy Sparkes, Marcus P. S. Badger
item.description:
Science Advances — matched: ice sheet, cryosphere, Antarctic, ocean circulation, carbon cycle
The Middle Miocene expansion of the Antarctic Ice Sheet coincides with major sedimentological changes in Malta. This interval also saw reorganisations in ocean circulation linked to closure of the Mesopotamian Seaway (MSR-events) and perturbations in the carbon cycle (CM events). The final CM event (CM-6), slightly lags the main glacial phase and remains difficult to interpret due to competing mechanisms and conflicting p CO 2 reconstructions. To explore links between cryosphere, circulation, hydroclimate, and the carbon cycle, we present new geochemical records from Malta. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. The results indicate a shift toward stronger monsoonal influence, delivering enhanced freshwater and nutrient fluxes to the region. This enhanced local biological carbon pump may have acted as a positive feedback to a global CO 2 drawdown. However, any contribution to global CO 2 drawdown remains tentative and cannot be confirmed without contemporaneous high-resolution open-ocean records.

item.title: The evolution of Upper Circumpolar Deep Water in the Southwest Pacific Ocean since 30 ka: evidence from Neodymium isotopes
item.dc:creator: Xiaojie Tang, Giuseppe Siani, Christophe Colin, Élisabeth Michel, Bruno Millet, Rosella Pinna‐Jamme, … (+2)
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: Antarctic, Southern Ocean, last glacial maximum, Holocene
The geometry and ventilation of upper deep-water masses in the Pacific sector of the Southern Ocean are critical to glacial carbon storage, yet their evolution since the Last Glacial Maximum remains poorly constrained. Here, we present the foraminiferal neodymium isotope composition (ε Nd ) from core MD97-2115 (eastern Chatham Rise, 2160 m water depth), which is located at the present-day boundary between Upper Circumpolar Deep Water (UCDW) and modified North Pacific Deep Water (mNPDW) in the Southwest Pacific, to reconstruct the upper deep-water mass changes since 30 ka. Combining quantitative binary mixing calculations with vertical ε Nd gradients relative to Lower Circumpolar Deep Water, we suggest substantial shifts in the geometry and mixing of UCDW and mNPDW since 30 ka. The variation phases include reduced UCDW influence during 30–20 ka, enhanced UCDW contribution between 20 and 14.3 ka, slightly decreased UCDW during 14.3–11.4 ka, and stable Holocene conditions. The glacial dominance of mNPDW is consistent with basin-wide evidence for enhanced storage of respired carbon in Pacific-sourced deep waters, likely contributing to the maintenance of low atmospheric CO 2 during the glacial period. Crucially, the early rapid increase in UCDW at ∼20 ka preceded the penetration of North Atlantic-sourced water into Southern Ocean and the deglacial CO 2 increase by several millennia, implying a critical role for Antarctic and Southern Ocean processes in establishing the oceanic precondition for glacial termination. During the last deglacial period, the decoupling between our reconstruction and atmospheric CO 2 evolution suggests that water-mass geometry alone is insufficient to drive the full deglacial CO 2 increase, pointing to additional roles for processes such as regional outgassing and variability in air–sea gas exchange efficiency.

item.title: Contrasting Terminus Dynamics of Lake-Terminating Glaciers in Lago Argentino (Patagonia), 2016–2026: A Training-Free Sentinel-2/Sentinel-1 Workflow
item.dc:creator: Carmen Fattore, Jairo R. Coronado-Hernández
item.description:
Geomatics — matched: glacier, iceberg
Lake-terminating glaciers of the Southern Patagonian Icefield are retreating rapidly, yet dense multi-glacier records of their termini remain scarce. We present a training-free workflow in Google Earth Engine that measures ice-area change within a fixed terminus domain from every usable Sentinel-2 scene (per-scene Otsu threshold on the near-infrared band, with cloud screening restricted to lake pixels) and delineates annual terminus positions automatically. Applied to Perito Moreno, Upsala and Spegazzini glaciers (Lago Argentino, Argentina) for October–March 2016–2026, it yielded 260 scenes. Perito Moreno showed no significant trend until mid-2019 and then lost 0.39 km2 a−1 (p < 0.001); its terminus retreated by about 580 m in nine summers; the two most recent summers showed the largest seasonal losses of the record (≈1.6–1.7 km2); and in March 2026 the front detached from Península de Magallanes. Upsala retreated by about 1010 m (≈130 m a−1), whereas Spegazzini remained within ±100 m of its 2017 position. Warm, dry summers in 2021–2022 affected all three glaciers, so their contrasting responses suggest that basin geometry and lateral support modulate the response to a common climate. Sentinel-1 reproduced the Perito Moreno decline but failed in iceberg-choked Brazo Upsala.
